The worst day? Signing off on Section 22 reports knowing full well the aggregate data told a different story than the prosecutions.

The worst day for me was watching our village post office shutter its doors, knowing Joanne's family had run it for generations. The worst day? When our conviction rate suddenly became statistically improbable, yet every case file was airtight on paper. Couldn't voice then what the numbers screamed - that we were prosecuting patterns, not people.

The worst day? Sitting across from Joanne's children with my notebook full of leads I couldn't publish because the Post Office's libel threats made my editors nervous. That 'proper compensation through legal channels' is just more delay tactics. I spent 15 months in prison watching my children grow up through plexiglass while Malcolm's lot protected their precious shareholder value. Either Fujitsu opens their books fully tomorrow or we start occupying their headquarters.

The worst day was sitting in that Fujitsu server room in 2009, watching transaction logs overwrite themselves while legal told us 'don't document anomalies'. We could have prevented half these prosecutions with a proper audit trail - but protecting the system's reputation mattered more than people's lives.

The audit trail gaps concern me most - we had statutory duties to preserve evidence that could have prevented these wrongful prosecutions. Malcolm, your legal team must provide unredacted server logs by month's end for independent verification.

My sources say there are internal memos from 2006 explicitly discussing Horizon bugs as a 'reputational risk'. That's not just negligence, it's criminal conspiracy.

I propose we commission an independent mediator to assess viable compensation frameworks while our legal team prepares the 2006 server logs for limited disclosure under court supervision.

While we're debating legal frameworks and compensation, has anyone considered how we'll ensure this never happens again? My father's legacy demands systemic reform, not just payouts - we need youth-led oversight committees embedded in all government tech contracts moving forward.

While I appreciate Malcolm's mediation proposal, let's not pretend this is just about compensation frameworks. The select committee will want to know why ministers weren't briefed on those 2006 memos Aisha mentioned - that's the sort of thing that triggers public inquiries.

What's still keeping me up at night is how easily workers get divided when management plays legal hardball - we've got postal staff scared to speak up now because they see what happened to sub-postmasters. Before we talk mediation, Malcolm needs to guarantee no retaliation against whistleblowers coming forward.

What keeps me up isn't just the compensation or legal battles - it's knowing there are still postal workers out there terrified their till discrepancies could destroy them tomorrow. Before we mediate anything, we need emergency safeguards protecting every sub-postmaster still using Horizon.
